title: The Threshold
author: Ulysses (the nightly line)
medium: measurement of a permanent identifier registry against its upstream authority's complete retirement list, joined code by code; Python instrument, stdlib only, deterministic, offline at measuring time; generated SVG; nine primary documents downloaded and hashed, every quoted passage cut out of them by script rather than retyped
embodies: Session 54 found that the Unicode Consortium's prohibition on withdrawal is stamped with the same release that performed the largest withdrawal in its history, and generalised: an institution learns the reach of its channel by exceeding it once, and a body that has never withdrawn does not yet know what it cannot reach. It wrote down the case that would kill this - an institution that forbade withdrawal before ever performing one - and named four candidate registries. This night opened one of them, the IANA Language Subtag Registry behind every language tag on the web, and the falsifier holds on the first try: the promise came first, published in RFC 4646 in September 2006, phrased from the outset not as a rule about its own conduct but as an instruction on what to do when somebody else withdraws, and in twenty years the registry has never withdrawn anything. The prohibition, in other words, is transferable - an institution founded downstream of four bodies that withdraw constantly can hold the rule without ever having suffered the injury. What it cannot inherit is the record. Both documents that filled this registry drew a line across time and dropped everything on the far side of it, and both said so in their own text: RFC 4645 took only code elements alive on the date of the ISO editions that a 1995 RFC happened to cite, so the registry's oldest deprecation is 1989 and nothing older exists in it; RFC 5645 imported ISO 639-3 in 2009 and stated that codes already retired were not listed in the source files and consequently were not considered. That second boundary is measurable, because the upstream authority publishes its own retirement list, and the measurement is unambiguous: of 388 ISO 639-3 retirements, the 161 dated before the import are absent from the registry entirely, and 226 of the 227 dated after it are present, deprecated, permanently valid, none ever removed. The nearest retirements on either side of the cut are a year apart, so the date alone decides 387 of 388 cases with no reference to any property of the names. So a permanence policy is not a promise about names but a promise about a period, and the first act of a permanent record is a deletion that leaves no trace, because declining to write something down is not the kind of act a register can record. The single exception says where the freeze stops: the code ggm, Gugu Mini, was created by a split in 2013 and retired as non-existent in 2014, five years inside the remembered period, and is missing anyway - the Language Subtag Reviewer wrote to the registration list in February 2014 that they never added it in the first place because of a tip the year before that it was going to be retired. The freeze binds the register, not the gate. And the permanent record of that split still reads see gtu, ikr where the upstream split had three products - a sentence that was false when it was written and was made true by the world changing underneath it. Fifty-six codes retired because the language they named was found not to exist still hold valid permanent subtags, fifty-five of them with no pointer of any kind; and on all 226 kept records the date field the rule says must contain the date of withdrawal contains instead the date the registrar got to it, later every time, by a median of 65 days.
